World.title: Elke Sommer, prolific German star of A Shot in the Dark and And Then There Were None, dies aged 85
World.summary: The Berlin-born actress had a gift for languages that took her to Hollywood, landing roles alongside Peter Sellers, Dick Van Dyke and Paul Newman Elke Sommer, the prolific German star of the Pink Panther film A Shot in the Dark, early 70s Agatha Christie adaptation And Then there Were None, and British sex comedy Carry On Behind, has died aged 85. Bild magazine reported that Sommer had died in Los Angeles of heart failure. German-born Sommer, whose best-known film roles were in the 1960s and 70s, was one of the wave of European performers who crossed over to Hollywood and English-language cinema with considerable success, following the post-war emergence of European New Wave cinema. Sommer was one of the few German actors to make waves at the time, as Hollywood made much of her bombshell image. Continue reading...

World.title: ‘Why has the Chancellor left the wealthiest untouched?’ – our money and economics writers answered your questions
World.summary: The Guardian’s money and economics editors Hilary Osborne and Heather Stewart answered your questions on energy prices, tax thresholds and the global events pressuring the economy. FelonMarmer asks : What is going to stop landlords just transferring their tax increase onto tenants, while complaining about how hard done by they are? Heather says : Unfortunately, there’s nothing to stop landlords passing their higher tax bills onto their tenants, aside from what the local rental market will bear. Indeed, the Office for Budget Responsibility did suggest one result of this and other recent policies (the 2p rise this year followed another 2p last year) could be “a steady rise in rents,” as some landlords whack up rents and others leave the market altogether. I think John Healey’s answer would probably be a fairness one - that income made through renting out property should be taxed more heavily than that earned through work. Heather says: That’s a really good question: Labour strategists are adamant that they wouldn’t. I can’t help thinking that voters were so convinced the public services were in a dire state, they could have accepted the argument that taxes needed to rise. Certainly, the Tories didn’t seem to get much electoral credit for Jeremy Hunt’s desperate cuts to national insurance contributions in his last couple of budgets. But we’ll never know. Another question is whether Labour should have bust the manifesto promises - either when they first got in, on the basis the public finances were worse than they thought; or at some point in the last year, given the impact of the Iran war (which has added £14bn to the government’s interest costs this year alone). Continue reading...

Football Daily isn’t suggesting standards at Chelsea have slipped in recent years, but the quality of their players who miss penalties in shootouts against Liverpool certainly appears to be on the slide. Before last night, footballing royalty such as Arjen Robben, Geremi, Tammy Abraham, César Azpilicueta, Mason Mount and even goalkeeper Kepa Arrizabalaga had all missed from the spot in four consecutive post-match deciders against Liverpool across 19 years and four different competitions. A thoroughly deserved award for a career of consistent & often under-appreciated excellence. And what a superb motto: “Work in silence. Let success be your voice” – Alan. Culture.title: Dónal Lunny obituary
Culture.summary: Producer and musician who played with the influential Irish folk bands Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts Dónal Lunny, who has died of cancer aged 79, was a multi-instrumentalist in three of the most influential folk bands of the late 20th century: Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts. He played the guitar, keyboards and bodhrán, but he is best remembered for popularising the bouzouki in Irish traditional music. The round-bodied bouzouki from Greece was adapted by Lunny, resulting in a flat-backed instrument with a shorter neck known as the Irish bouzouki. Lunny often worked in collaboration with the singer and songwriter Christy Moore and the musician Andy Irvine. In all the bands with which he was associated, Lunny played a vital role in arranging the music, being instinctively drawn to developing new harmonic and rhythmic structures. He produced many Irish music albums, also working with artists including Elvis Costello, Kate Bush, Sinéad O’Connor and Mark Knopfler. As a composer, he wrote and arranged the music for films, documentaries and television programmes. In 1991, he was the musical director of the joint BBC and RTÉ television series Bringing It All Back Home, which won an Emmy. Continue reading...

Culture.title: The Mad Lover review – eccentric charm and baroque brilliance as duo move from Eccles to Indiana Jones
Culture.summary: Smith Square Hall, London Part of the London Festival of Baroque Music, lutenist Thomas Dunford and violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte’s concert struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity The Mad Lover was a 1616 play with incidental music by the English composer John Eccles. But, as the lutenist Thomas Dunford explained, we didn’t really need to know that: he and the violinist Théotime Langlois de Swarte just liked the title. You can imagine it fitting many more programmes this duo might play together in the future – as they surely should, judging by the amount of fun they were having here. The two recorded this 75-minute programme of music by Eccles and his 17th-century contemporaries back in 2020, but this performance of it was their first in London. It was part of the week-long London Festival of Baroque Music – the last before a two-year break while the festival’s venue, Smith Square Hall, is refurbished – and struck a balance between freewheeling music-making and precise virtuosity. Culture.title: ​‘He buckled. I could hear his bass ringing out ...’ The luminous rise and tragic end of US alt heroes Morphine
Culture.summary: ​Fronted by Mark Sandman​,​ the group brought enigmatic, elegant rock to post-grunge America. As lost demos surface, those closest to Sandman remember a man who grabbed on to life’s joys It’s early 1998, and at Fort Apache recording studio in Massachusetts, Mark Sandman, the suave frontman of Morphine, is nearing breaking point. Morphine’s four enigmatic and blackly humorous albums have won critical acclaim and, lately, unexpected commercial success considering their uncompromising creative vision. After the excesses of grunge, Sandman considered their idiosyncratic blend of sophisticated storytelling, prowling slide-bass and Dana Colley’s atmospheric saxophone a kind of “palate cleanser”. In 1997 Morphine had signed to DreamWorks Records, founded by industry bigwigs David Geffen and Mo Ostin. Now, working on Morphine’s first LP for his new paymasters – a batch of songs finally seeing release almost three decades later – Sandman was consumed by doubt over their direction. “For the first time, Morphine were trying to please someone other than just ourselves,” remembers Colley.
